Define some functions to avoid repetition of same processes

calculate_outliers <- function(data) {
  # Check for regular outliers
  outliers <- boxplot.stats(data)$out
  num_outliers <- length(outliers)

  # Calculate the lower and upper bounds for severe outliers
  Q1 <- quantile(data, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)
  Q3 <- quantile(data, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
  IQR <- Q3 - Q1

  lower_severe_bound <- Q1 - 3 * IQR
  upper_severe_bound <- Q3 + 3 * IQR

  # Identify severe outliers
  severe_outliers <- data[data < lower_severe_bound | data > upper_severe_bound]
  num_severe_outliers <- length(severe_outliers)

  # Return the results as a list
  return(list(
    num_outliers = num_outliers,
    num_severe_outliers = num_severe_outliers
  ))
}

summary_and_normality_check <- function(data) {
  #Basic summary 
  print("Summary: ")
  print(summary(data))
  
  # Plot normality 
  print("Mean")
  mm <- mean(data); print(mm)
  print("Standard deviation")
  ss <- sd(data); print(ss)
  hist(data,freq = F,100, main = "Histogram")
  curve(dnorm(x, mean = mm, sd = ss),col="red", lwd = 2, add=T)
  
  #Compute skewness
  print("Skewness")
  print(skewness(data))
  
  #Number of outliers
  print("Outliers: ")
  print(calculate_outliers(data))
  
  #Shapiro test
  print("Shapiro test: ")
  print(shapiro.test(data))

}

Data Preparation

In this section, a descriptive analysis is conducted on each variable, a data quality report is generated, and imputation and profiling are addressed.

Univariate Descriptive Analysis (Variable Analysis)

  • Original numeric variables corresponding to qualitative concepts have to be converted to factors:
  • Original numeric variables corresponding to real quantitative concepts are kept as numeric but additional factors should also be created
  • Exploratory Data Analysis for each variable (numeric summary and graphic support) of the train sample.

Variable avganncount

avganncount is a numerical variable representing the “Mean number of reported cancer cases diagnosed annually (2010-2015).” The difference between the mean (623.2) and the median (175) indicates that the distribution is not symmetric and deviates from normality. Additionally, the first and third quartiles (80 and 509, respectively) are much lower than the mean of 623.2 and the maximum value of 38150.0, further suggesting skewness. The boxplot confirms this skewness, with an extended upper whisker and numerous outliers, indicating a heavy right tail. It has 273 outliers, and 224 of these are severe outliers.

The histogram overlaid with a normal curve highlights the deviation from a normal distribution with the same mean and standard deviation. This variable has no missing values. Lastly, the skeweness indicator and Shapiro test rejection of the null hypothesis also confirm the non-normal distribution of the variable.

– anna – In this variable there are 126 values = “1962.667684” we should consider these as NA

variable <- train$avganncount
summary <- summary(variable); summary
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##     7.0    80.0   175.0   623.2   509.0 38150.0
variable[variable == 453.5494221] <- NA
summary <- summary(variable); summary
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##     7.0    80.0   175.0   623.2   509.0 38150.0
mm <- mean(variable)
ss <- sd(variable)
range <- (summary[[6]] - summary[[1]]); range
## [1] 38143
boxplot(variable, main = "Boxplot")

hist(variable,freq = F,100, main = "Histogram")
curve(dnorm(x, mean = mm, sd = ss),col="red", lwd = 2, add=T)

shapiro.test(variable)
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  variable
## W = 0.33377, p-value < 2.2e-16
calculate_outliers(variable)
## $num_outliers
## [1] 273
## 
## $num_severe_outliers
## [1] 224

Variable avgdeathsperyear

In a similar way, avgdeathsperyear is a numerical variable expressing the “Mean number of reported mortalities due to cancer”.

It has no missing values. The difference between the mean (191.6) and median (62) indicates that the distribution is not symmetric. Moreover, the first and third quartiles (29 and 140.5, respectivelly) are lower than the mean and the maximum value of 14010, further suggesting a skewed ditribution. With the help of graphical tools like the boxplot we can confirm the skeweness, obtaining 225 outliers (138 of which are severe), indicating a large right tail. The histogram overlaid with a normal curve highlights the deviation from a normal distribution with the same mean and standard deviation, and the Shapiro test also confirms the non-normality of the variable.

variable <- train$avgdeathsperyear;
summary <- summary(variable);summary
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.

mm <- mean(variable)
ss <- sd(variable)
range <- (summary[[6]] - summary[[1]]); range

boxplot(variable, main = "Boxplot")

hist(variable,freq = F,100, main = "Histogram")
curve(dnorm(x, mean = mm, sd = ss),col="red", lwd = 2, add=T)

skewness(variable)
## [1] 12.4999
shapiro.test(variable)
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  variable
## W = 0.26769, p-value < 2.2e-16
calculate_outliers(variable)
## $num_outliers

Variable target_deathrate :

Variable target_deathrate is a numerical variable that is the target of the model. It contains no missing values in the train sample. The median (178.3) and mean (178.8) values are really close, expressing the symmetry of the distribution of the variable. Thanks to the boxplot and the histogram we can graphically confirm the symmetry of the distribution.

We performed the Shapiro test to check for the normality of the data, and obtained a small p-value that rejects the null hypothesis, indicating that the variable does not follow a normal distribution. Therefore, the target variable is not normally distributed.

Moreover, it contains 35 outliers, 1 of which is a severe.

summary <- summary(variable); summary

curve(dnorm(x, mean = mm, sd = ss),col="red", lwd = 2, add=T)

skewness(variable)
## [1] 0.3243216
shapiro.test(variable)
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  variable
## W = 0.98647, p-value = 4.149e-12
calculate_outliers(variable)

## [1] 35

Variable incidencerate :

Variable incidencerate is a numerical variable that expresses “Mean per capita (100,000) cancer diagnoses”.

The variable has no missing values. It has similar mean (449) and median (453.5) values given its range and suggesting a simmetry distribution. It contains 60 outliers, 7 of which are severe outliers. In the boxplot we can see how the most severe outliers are high and not low values, corresponding to Osceola County, Florida and Williamsburg city, Virginia. The histogram with the overlapping normal distribution shows a quite symmetrical distribution, but the Shapiro test and skeweness value discard the normality of the variable’s distribution.

Variable popest2015 :

Variable popest2015 is a numerical variable that expresses the population of the county.

It does not count with missing values. It has a long range and is highly skewed, with a long right tail. In fact, it contains 252 outliers, 162 of which are severe, and all of them are above the upper whisker in the boxplot. The highest value is for Los Angeles County, California. The large difference between the mean (106.841) and median (27.158), along with the spread between the 1st (12.191) and 3rd quartiles (66.880), indicates a positively skewed distribution, where extreme high values are pulling the mean upward.

Variable povertypercent is a numerical variable that expresses the percent of population in poverty and has no missing values.

Variable studypercap : I CONSIDER IT IS WORTH TO REMOVE

Variable studypercap is a numerical variable that expresses “Per capita number of cancer-related clinical trials per county”.

It contains no missing values, and has 307 outliers (222 severe). Its distribution is non-symmetric. Note that 1162 out of 1831 observations contain value 0 in this variable, which indicates that it may only provide noise to the model. Thus, we consider it is worth to remove the variable. 

variable <- train$studypercap;
summary <- summary(variable); summary

mm <- mean(variable)
ss <- sd(variable)
range <- (summary[[6]] - summary[[1]]); range
## [1] 9762.309
Boxplot(variable, main = "Boxplot")

calculate_outliers(variable)

Variable medianage :

Medianage is a numerical variable that expresses the median age of county residents.

The variable has no missing values. Has 65 outliers, 18 of which are severe outliers. All of these outliers should be removed because it’s impossible to be more than 100 years. Once we removed all the incorrect values we get 52 outliers, 18 of then severe. Finally we observe a symmetric distribution with a median = 40.90 and a mean=40.85. After analyzing the boxplot, and the histogram along the Shapiro test we can discard the normality of the variable’s distribution.

variable <- train$medianage
summary <- summary(variable) ; summary
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##   23.30   37.90   40.90   45.25   44.00  624.00
calculate_outliers(variable)
## $num_outliers
## [1] 65
## 
## $num_severe_outliers
## [1] 18
variable[variable > 80] <- NA  # Replace values greater than 80 with NA
summary <- summary(variable) ; summary
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
##   23.30   37.90   40.90   40.85   43.80   59.00      18
mm <- mean(variable)
ss <- sd(variable)
range <- (summary[[6]] - summary[[1]]); range
## [1] 35.7
Boxplot(variable, main = "Boxplot")

##  [1] 1615   12  562  168  741 1810  254 1641 1607 1670  123  662 1016  632 1148
## [16]  112  178  208  865 1647
hist(variable,freq = F,100, main = "Histogram")
curve(dnorm(x, mean = mm, sd = ss) ,col="red", lwd = 2, add=T)

calculate_outliers(variable)
## $num_outliers
## [1] 52
## 
## $num_severe_outliers
## [1] 18
shapiro.test(variable)
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  variable
## W = 0.9951, p-value = 1.161e-05

Variable percentmarried

Numerical variable that represent the percent of county residents who are married.

It has a non-symmetric distribution, it is skewed with a long left tail observed in the histogram. It doesn’t have missing values, it has 34 outliers (non of them severe) and they are concentrated on the lower end of the distribution. With the shapiro-test we can confirm the rejection of the null hypothesis, therefore it doesn’t have a normal distribution.

variable <- train$percentmarried
summary <- summary(variable) ; summary
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##    23.1    47.8    52.5    51.9    56.4    68.0
sum(is.nan(variable))
## [1] 0
mm <- mean(variable)
ss <- sd(variable)
range <- (summary[[6]] - summary[[1]]); range
## [1] 44.9
Boxplot(variable, main = "Boxplot")

##  [1] 1468  718  168 1525  723  534  719  731  101 1623
hist(variable,freq = F,100, main = "Histogram")
curve(dnorm(x, mean = mm, sd = ss),col="red", lwd = 2, add=T)

calculate_outliers(variable)
## $num_outliers
## [1] 34
## 
## $num_severe_outliers
## [1] 0
shapiro.test(variable)
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  variable
## W = 0.97753, p-value = 2.346e-16

Variable pctnohs18_24

Numerical variable that show the percentage of county residents aged 18-24 whose highest level of education is less than a high school diploma.

The distribution of this variable is skewed with a long right tail, we can confirm that it doesn’t have a normal distribution thanks to the histogram and the curve. Moreover the p-value obtained in the shapiro-test confirm the non normal distribution. It doesn’t have misssing values, and it has 35 outliers, 5 of them severe.

variable <- train$pctnohs18_24
summary <- summary(variable); summary
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##    0.50   12.90   17.20   18.29   22.70   59.10
mm <- mean(variable)
ss <- sd(variable)

Boxplot(variable, main="Boxplot")

##  [1]  101 1168 1227 1468  372 1135 1692 1675 1736 1171
hist(variable , freq=F, 100, main="Histogram")
curve(dnorm(x,mean=mm,sd=ss),col='red', lwd=2, add = T)

calculate_outliers(variable)
## $num_outliers
## [1] 35
## 
## $num_severe_outliers
## [1] 5
shapiro.test(variable)
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  variable
## W = 0.96205, p-value < 2.2e-16

Variable ppcths18_24

Numeric variable, it represent the percentage of county residents ages 18-24 highest education attained is a high school diploma.

We can observe with the median(34,7%) and the mean(35%) that the variable has a symmetric distribuition, but after the shapiro_test we observe that it doesn’t have a normal distribution. It doesn’t have missing values and it has 33 outliers, non of them severe.

variable <- train$pcths18_24

summary <- summary(variable); summary
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##     0.0    29.2    34.7    35.0    40.5    72.5
mm <- mean(variable)
ss <- sd(variable)

Boxplot(variable, main="Boxplot")

##  [1]  101  106  131  168  294  389  642  741  786 1810 1636  555 1623 1709  443
## [16] 1716  436 1699 1155   70
hist(variable , freq=F, 100, main="Histogram")
curve(dnorm(x,mean=mm,sd=ss),col='red', lwd=2, add = T)

calculate_outliers(variable)
## $num_outliers
## [1] 33
## 
## $num_severe_outliers
## [1] 0
shapiro.test(variable)
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  variable
## W = 0.99323, p-value = 1.922e-07

Variable pctsomecol18_24 NOT WORTH TO USE IT (75% MISSING VALUES)

It has 1375 missing values. (75%) therefore we would remove this variable.

variable <- train$pctsomecol18_24

Variable pcths25_over

Numerical variable that express the percentage of county residents ages 25 and over highest education attained a high school diploma.

It doesn’t have missing values but it have 18 outliers, non of the severe. It doesn’t have a normal distribution.

variable <- train$pcths25_over
summary <- summary(variable); summary
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##    8.30   30.35   35.30   34.73   39.65   52.70
mm <- mean(variable)
ss <- sd(variable)

Boxplot(variable, main="Boxplot")

##  [1] 574 104 654 636 588 128 529 527 628 941
hist(variable , freq=F, 100, main="Histogram")
curve(dnorm(x,mean=mm,sd=ss),col='red', lwd=2, add = T)

skewness(variable)
## [1] -0.3660496
calculate_outliers(variable)
## $num_outliers
## [1] 18
## 
## $num_severe_outliers
## [1] 0
shapiro.test(variable)
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  variable
## W = 0.99107, p-value = 3.741e-09

Variable pctachdeg25_over

Numerical variable that expresses the the percentage of country resident ages 25 and over highest education attained: Bachelor’s degree.

Firstly we can see that there is a huge left skewness and there is a relatively large number of outliers (62), from which just 3 are severe. From the plot we can already tell that no normal distribution is followed and a shapiro test over the variable confirms it.

summary_and_normality_check(train$pctbachdeg25_over)

Variable pctunemployed16_over

Numerical variable that represents the percentage of county residents ages 16 and over, unemployed.

This variable is heavily left skewed and contains over 46 outliers, of which 4 are severe. Despite the distrirbution looking almost normal there is a big number of outliers and a long heavy right tail. Applying a shapiro test we reject the hypothesis that the distribution is normal.

summary_and_normality_check(train$pctunemployed16_over)
## [1] "Summary: "
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##   0.700   5.500   7.500   7.861   9.750  29.400

## [1] "Skewness"
## [1] 0.9189968
## [1] "Outliers: "
## $num_outliers

## 
## $num_severe_outliers

##

Variable pctprivatecoveragealone

Numerical variable that represents the percentage of county residents with private health coverage alone (no public assistance at all).

The number of NA is humongous (356), but it has a small amount of mild outliers (4) and almost no skewness at all. Both using inferential and visualizations methods we cannot easily reject the hypothesis that this variable is not normal. So we can loosely say that is normally distributed.

summary_and_normality_check(na.omit(train$pctprivatecoveragealone))

Variable pctempprivcoverage

Numerical variable that represents the percentage of county residents with employee-provided private health coverage.

Despite the low number of outliers (7 mild), the absence of NA, the small left skewness and the median being almost equal to the mean, we should reject the null hypothesis that the distribution is normal with a 5% significance. However, with a smaller significance level than 2.5% we couldn’t reject that this distribution is not normal. Almost normal

Variable pctpubliccoveragealone

Numerical variable that represents the percent of county residents with government-provided health coverage alone.

This variable contains 21 mild outliers, a great left skewness and a long right tail. Performing an inferential test like shapiro we get a tiny p-value which makes us reject the hypothesis that the distribution is normal under any significance level.

Variable pctwhite

Numerical variable that represents the percent of county residents who identify as White.

Both from the plot and from inferential methods we can easily discard that this variable is anywhere near normal, being a hugely right skewed variable. It contains 104 outliers from which 7 are severe.

This points out that the vast majority of counties have a high percentage of white population.

Variable pctblack

Numerical variable that represents the percent of county residents who identify as Black.

There is a huge number of outliers (323), from which 99 are severe and there is also a huge left skewness, that points out that the vast majority of counties (except the outliers) have a rather low percentage of black folks. The distribution almost looks like a power law distribution (Zipf) therefore we can safely reject both with visualization and inferential methods that the distribution of this variable is not normal.

summary_and_normality_check(train$pctblack)
